title: Three equations. One solution.
caption: Gaussian elimination turns a tangled system into a staircase.
voice: Three equations and three unknowns. Where should we start? Instead of guessing values, we can reorganize the equations until the answer becomes easy to read. This is Gaussian elimination. In this video, we will solve one three by three system, understand pivots, and recover the unknowns using back substitution.

title: Meet the system
caption: x, y and z are unknown numbers. Each equation is one constraint.
voice: Here is our system. x plus y plus z equals six. Two x plus three y plus z equals eleven. Three x plus two y plus five z equals twenty two. We need one ordered triple that satisfies all three equations at the same time. We will keep the variable order x, y, z throughout.

title: A geometric picture
caption: Each equation represents a plane in three-dimensional space.
voice: Think of each equation as a plane in three dimensional space. A solution must lie on every plane. In this example, the three planes meet at a single point. Elimination changes the equations into simpler ones while keeping exactly the same common intersection. The point stays fixed even when a plane changes.

title: Why row operations are allowed
caption: Every allowed operation is reversible, so the solution set is preserved.
voice: Three operations are allowed. Swap two equations. Multiply an equation by a nonzero number. Or add a multiple of one equation to another. Each operation is reversible. For example, after replacing row two by row two minus twice row one, adding twice row one restores the original row. That is why we do not lose solutions.

title: Write the augmented matrix
caption: [A | b]: coefficients on the left, right-hand-side constants on the right.
voice: Now record just the coefficients and constants in an augmented matrix. The columns correspond to x, y, and z. The vertical bar separates the coefficient matrix A from the constant vector b. Each row still represents one whole equation. Whenever we change a row, we must also change its constant on the right.

title: Choose the first pivot
caption: A pivot is the leading nonzero entry used to eliminate entries below it.
voice: The first entry is one. We use it as our first pivot. Our immediate goal is to make the two entries below it zero. This removes x from the second and third equations. We keep the first row unchanged and use multiples of it to cancel the two and the three below the pivot.

title: Eliminate the 2 below the pivot
caption: R2 ← R2 − 2R1. Apply the operation to all four entries.
voice: Replace row two by row two minus twice row one. Entry by entry, two minus two is zero. Three minus two is one. One minus two is negative one. And eleven minus twelve is negative one. The new second row is zero, one, negative one, negative one. It represents y minus z equals negative one.

title: Eliminate the 3 below the pivot
caption: R3 ← R3 − 3R1. The first column is now cleared below the pivot.
voice: Next replace row three by row three minus three times row one. Three minus three is zero. Two minus three is negative one. Five minus three is two. Twenty two minus eighteen is four. So the third row becomes zero, negative one, two, four. Both lower equations are now free of x.

title: Move to the second pivot
caption: The second pivot is in column y. Clear the entry directly below it.
voice: Move one row down and one column right. The one in row two is our second pivot. There is a negative one below it. Adding row two to row three will cancel that entry. Notice the staircase taking shape. Each new pivot must appear to the right of the pivot in the row above.

title: Create the final zero
caption: R3 ← R3 + R2. Now the last equation contains only z.
voice: Replace row three by row three plus row two. Zero plus zero stays zero. Negative one plus one is zero. Two plus negative one is one. Four plus negative one is three. The last row is now zero, zero, one, three. We have reached row echelon form: all entries below the three pivots are zero.

title: Read the staircase
caption: Forward elimination is complete. This is echelon form, not reduced echelon form.
voice: Translate the rows back into equations. x plus y plus z equals six. y minus z equals negative one. And z equals three. This triangular structure is the purpose of forward elimination. We did not need to make the entries above each pivot zero. Instead, we can now solve from the bottom upward.

title: Back substitution: solve for z
caption: Start at the bottom: 1z = 3, so z = 3.
voice: Start with the last equation. One times z equals three, so z equals three. This is our first known value. Back substitution means taking a value we have just found and inserting it into an earlier equation. With z known, the second equation contains only one unknown, y.

title: Back substitution: solve for y
caption: y − z = −1 → y − 3 = −1 → y = 2.
voice: The second equation says y minus z equals negative one. Substitute z equals three. We get y minus three equals negative one. Add three to both sides, and y equals two. Watch how the known z value travels upward from the third row into the second. We now know two of our three unknowns.

title: Back substitution: solve for x
caption: x + y + z = 6 → x + 2 + 3 = 6 → x = 1.
voice: Finally, use the first equation. x plus y plus z equals six. Substitute y equals two and z equals three. Then x plus five equals six, so x equals one. Our candidate solution is the ordered triple one, two, three. The upward substitution has recovered every unknown without any guesswork.

title: Verify in the original equations
caption: Check the original system, not just the transformed matrix.
voice: Always verify the answer in the original system. One plus two plus three equals six. Two times one, plus three times two, plus three equals eleven. Three times one, plus two times two, plus five times three equals twenty two. All three checks pass, so our solution is correct.

title: Why is the answer unique?
caption: Three pivot columns for three unknowns means there are no free variables.
voice: There is one pivot in each of the three variable columns. So there are no free variables, and this system has exactly one solution. Geometrically, the common intersection is one point. This conclusion is specific to our example. Other systems can have no solution or infinitely many solutions, depending on their final rows.

title: Two other possible endings
caption: A contradiction means no solution. A free variable in a consistent system gives infinitely many.
voice: For comparison, a row of zero, zero, zero, five means zero equals five. That is a contradiction, so there is no solution. A row of all zeros means zero equals zero and adds no constraint. If the system is consistent and a variable column has no pivot, a free variable remains and there are infinitely many solutions.

title: Three ideas to remember
caption: Preserve the solution set. Build a staircase. Substitute upward.
voice: Remember these three ideas. First, reversible row operations preserve the solution set. Second, forward elimination uses pivots to create zeros below them, building a staircase. Third, back substitution solves from the bottom upward. In our example, these steps gave x equals one, y equals two, and z equals three.

title: Try one step yourself
caption: Pause here: which row operation will eliminate the 4?
voice: Try a quick check of your understanding. Suppose the pivot is two, and the entry below it is four. Which row operation makes that lower entry zero? Pause and think. The answer is row two minus twice row one. The multiplier is the target entry divided by the pivot: four divided by two.
